strategies.name: Cross-Sectional Mean Reversion (Khandani-Lo Linear Long-Short)
strategies.one_line: Each day, short the stocks that outperformed the equal-weighted market and buy those that underperformed, weighted by the size of that relative move.
strategies.hypothesis: Short-horizon relative return reversal is compensation for supplying liquidity. When a stock moves sharply relative to its peers on no fundamental news, the move is largely the price impact of someone needing immediacy. A trader who takes the other side earns the liquidity premium as the impact decays. The mechanism is specific and testable: the edge should be larger in less liquid names, larger on high-volume days, and should have collapsed in August 2007 when many liquidity providers deleveraged simultaneously - which it did, and that event is itself evidence for the mechanism rather than against it.
strategies.universe: All members of a broad index (S&P 500, S&P 1500 or Russell 2000) as of each date, using point-in-time index membership to avoid survivorship bias.
strategies.entry_rule: Near the close of day t compute each stock's daily return r_i. Compute the equal-weighted mean return across the universe, r_bar. Set weight w_i = -(r_i - r_bar) / sum_k |r_k - r_bar|. Enter at the close of day t.
strategies.exit_rule: Fully liquidate and re-enter with new weights at the close of day t+1. Holding period is exactly one day; there is no separate exit signal.
strategies.position_sizing: Weights are self-normalising: gross exposure is always 1.0 of capital and the book is close to dollar-neutral by construction. No leverage assumed in the base case.

parameters.name: universe_size
parameters.what_it_controls: Liquidity and capacity. Smaller-cap universes historically show a larger effect and higher costs.

published.title: What Happened to the Quants in August 2007?
published.link: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1015987

strategies.replication_notes: Chan (2013) Example 4.3 reproduces it on SPX and reports it as a true out-of-sample test post-2007. Widely replicated.

claimed_performance.metric: APR / Sharpe
claimed_performance.value: 13.7% APR, Sharpe 1.3 on SPX (Chan's replication); Chan separately cites Sharpe 4.7 for the intraday variant
claimed_performance.source_note: Author's claim, gross of costs. Chan does not state a commission or slippage assumption for this figure.

strategies.known_decay: Chan reports a declining cumulative return profile within his own 2007-2011 sample. The strategy is the canonical example of a crowded liquidity-provision trade: Khandani and Lo's own paper documents its multi-sigma failure in August 2007 caused by simultaneous deleveraging. McLean and Pontiff (2016) find ~58% average post-publication decay across 97 predictors; this one was published in 2007 and has had ~19 years of exposure.
strategies.capacity_notes: Daily turnover is 200% of gross. Capacity is bounded by the liquidity it is harvesting - scaling up means becoming the crowd whose impact the strategy is paid to absorb. Fine at personal-account size; this is the class of strategy that works better small.
strategies.turnover: ~200% of gross per day (full liquidation and re-entry)
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Severe. At 200% daily turnover, a 0.05% round-trip cost consumes roughly 25% per year of gross return. The 13.7% gross APR does not survive a 0.1% round trip. This is the single most important thing to model.
strategies.shorting_leverage: Requires short sales of roughly half the book. Borrow cost data is unavailable locally, so the short-side contribution is unverifiable.
strategies.redundancy: Distinct from the trend-following work that produced nothing across 237 configurations - this is the opposite sign and a far shorter horizon. Overlaps conceptually with short-term reversal (st-reversal-1m) but at a 1-day rather than 1-month horizon.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible on its face. Paying someone to absorb an urgent trade is a real service with a real price, and the direction of the trade matches who needs what.
strategies.reason: Zero fitted parameters, a clean mechanism, fully testable on local data, and the cost question is the entire question - which makes it a fast and highly informative first test.

preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes 0.05% round-trip all-in cost on S&P 500 names and no short-borrow fee. I expect roughly a quarter of Chan's claimed gross figure to survive. The gap is almost entirely undisclosed transaction costs, and secondarily 19 years of post-publication crowding.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Chan claims 13.7% APR gross. I estimate low single digits net, possibly negative. The difference is transaction costs at 200% daily turnover, which he does not model in this example.

tweaks.change: Restrict the universe to the bottom liquidity tercile of the index rather than all members.
tweaks.why: The mechanism is liquidity provision, so the premium should concentrate where liquidity is scarcest. This changes the economics, not a threshold.
tweaks.disproof: If net Sharpe does not improve relative to the full universe after modelling the higher spreads in those names, the liquidity-premium mechanism is not what is generating the return.

tweaks.change: Condition entry on a market-wide dislocation measure (e.g. cross-sectional return dispersion above its 80th percentile) and stand aside otherwise.
tweaks.why: Liquidity demand is episodic. Holding the book every day pays full transaction costs for the many days on which no one needed immediacy.
tweaks.disproof: If the filtered version's net Sharpe is not materially above the always-on version, the edge is not concentrated in dislocation days and the turnover cannot be reduced this way.

tweaks.change: Replace the raw relative return with the residual from a contemporaneous factor regression (market, size, value, industry).
tweaks.why: Part of the raw relative return is factor exposure rather than idiosyncratic impact, so the raw signal takes unintended factor bets that are not the liquidity premium.
tweaks.disproof: If residualised weights produce lower gross returns with no volatility reduction, the factor exposure was contributing return rather than noise.

tweaks.change: Lengthen the holding period to 2-5 days with proportional position scaling.
tweaks.why: Directly attacks the cost problem by cutting turnover 2-5x.
tweaks.disproof: If gross return falls faster than turnover, the reversal is fully realised within one day and cannot be harvested more slowly.

strategies.name: Intraday Cross-Sectional Reversal (Close-to-Open Signal)
strategies.one_line: Use the overnight close-to-open return as the reversal signal, enter at the open and liquidate at the close the same day.
strategies.hypothesis: Same liquidity-provision mechanism as the daily version, but applied to the overnight gap. Overnight moves are formed in thin trading and disproportionately reflect order imbalance rather than information, so they should revert more reliably than close-to-close moves. Concentrating the holding period inside the regular session also removes overnight gap risk.
strategies.universe: Members of a broad index, point-in-time.
strategies.entry_rule: At the open of day t compute r_i = (open_t - close_{t-1}) / close_{t-1}. Compute the cross-sectional mean r_bar. Set w_i = -(r_i - r_bar) / sum_k |r_k - r_bar|. Enter at the open.
strategies.exit_rule: Liquidate the entire book at the close of the same day t.
strategies.position_sizing: Self-normalising to gross exposure 1.0, approximately dollar-neutral.

parameters.what_it_controls: Liquidity and the size of the effect.

strategies.replication_notes: Chan presents it as an enhancement of Khandani-Lo rather than an independently published result. No third-party replication located.

claimed_performance.metric: Sharpe
claimed_performance.value: Chan cites Sharpe 4.7 for the intraday cross-sectional mean reversion variant on SPX
claimed_performance.period: not precisely stated for this variant
claimed_performance.source_note: Author's claim, gross of costs. A Sharpe of 4.7 on a daily-rebalanced equity book is implausible net of realistic costs and should be treated as a gross upper bound, not a result.

strategies.known_decay: No dedicated decay study located. The parent strategy is heavily crowded. A Sharpe near 5 gross at 200% daily turnover is exactly the profile that is entirely consumed by costs, which is the most likely reason such a number can persist in print without being arbitraged.
strategies.capacity_notes: Lower than the daily version - execution must happen at or near the open, the least liquid and widest-spread moment of the session.
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Extreme. Entry is at the open, where spreads are widest. A Sharpe of 4.7 gross is compatible with a Sharpe near zero net.
strategies.shorting_leverage: Requires intraday short sales; locates at the open are the practical constraint. Borrow data unavailable.
strategies.redundancy: Direct variant of xs-mr-khandani-lo. Test one before the other; results will be highly correlated.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible. Overnight moves in thin markets containing more noise than information is a defensible claim.
strategies.reason: Mechanism is sound and it is cheap to test on local data, but the claimed Sharpe is not credible net of open-auction spreads, so it must be tested with an explicit and pessimistic cost model or the test says nothing.

preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes 0.10% round trip reflecting open-auction spreads. I think this is worth well under a fifth of the claimed figure.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Chan implies Sharpe 4.7; I estimate under 0.6 net. The gap is the open-auction spread, which is the dominant cost and is not modelled in his example.

tweaks.change: Enter 15-30 minutes after the open instead of at the open itself.
tweaks.why: Trades the first part of the reversal for a much narrower spread. Tests whether the edge is in the auction imbalance or persists past it.
tweaks.disproof: If the gross edge disappears by 09:45, the effect is purely an opening-auction artefact and is not capturable at retail spreads.

tweaks.change: Require the overnight gap to exceed a multiple of the stock's trailing overnight volatility before taking a position.
tweaks.why: Filters to gaps large enough to plausibly be impact rather than information, and cuts the number of positions and hence cost.
tweaks.disproof: If returns per dollar traded do not rise with the threshold, gap size is not proxying for order imbalance.

tweaks.change: Exclude names with an earnings announcement or scheduled news event overnight.
tweaks.why: Those gaps are information, not imbalance, and should not revert. Including them means systematically fading real news.
tweaks.disproof: If excluding them does not improve returns, the signal is not distinguishing news from noise and the stated mechanism is wrong.

strategies.name: Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
strategies.one_line: Buy stocks that gap up on an earnings announcement and short those that gap down, holding for the drift that follows.
strategies.hypothesis: Investors underreact to earnings news. The market moves part of the way to the new fundamental value on announcement day and the remainder over the following weeks, as attention is limited, analysts revise slowly and some holders face constraints that delay their trading. The anomaly has survived since Ball and Brown (1968), which is unusually long, and the persistence is usually attributed to limits to arbitrage - the names where drift is largest are small, illiquid and expensive to short.
strategies.universe: Stocks with a scheduled earnings announcement between the prior close and the current open, restricted to a liquid universe (e.g. price > $5, above a market-cap floor).
strategies.entry_rule: Compute retC2O = (open_t - close_{t-1}) / close_{t-1} for stocks announcing overnight. Compute stdC2O, the 90-day moving standard deviation of close-to-open returns for that stock. Go long at the open if retC2O >= 0.5 * stdC2O; go short if retC2O <= -0.5 * stdC2O.
strategies.exit_rule: Chan's base implementation exits at the close of the same day. The literature version holds 1 to 60 trading days; the standard test horizon is 60 days.
strategies.position_sizing: Equal dollar weight across all qualifying names, gross exposure divided by the number of positions (Chan divides by 30).

parameters.what_it_controls: How large a gap counts as a surprise; trades off signal strength against position count.

parameters.name: holding_period

published.authors: Ball, R. and Brown, P.; later Bernard, V. and Thomas, J. (1989)
published.title: An Empirical Evaluation of Accounting Income Numbers; Post-Earnings-Announcement Drift
published.link: https://www.jstor.org/stable/2490232

strategies.replication_notes: One of the most replicated anomalies in finance. Survives in Hou, Xue and Zhang (2020) in some specifications, which is notable given how many do not. Chan (2013) Example 7.2 gives a directly codeable version.

claimed_performance.metric: varies by study
claimed_performance.value: Chan does not state a headline figure for Example 7.2. The academic literature typically reports 5-10% annualised on a long-short 60-day drift portfolio.
claimed_performance.source_note: Author's claim. Figures vary widely by surprise definition (SUE vs gap vs analyst revision) and are usually gross.

strategies.known_decay: Well documented. The effect has attenuated substantially since the 1990s in large caps and now concentrates in small and illiquid names. Novy-Marx and Velikov (2016) place event-driven strategies of this turnover in the band where costs consume a large share of the gross spread.
strategies.capacity_notes: Capacity is limited by the announcement calendar and by the concentration of remaining drift in small caps. Adequate for a personal account.
strategies.data_gap: Requires earnings announcement dates with before-open versus after-close timing. The local database holds quarterly fundamentals with filing dates; whether it has announcement timestamps at that granularity is unverified and is the gating question for this entry.
strategies.turnover: Moderate - bounded by the number of announcements, roughly 4 events per name per year
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Moderate at a 60-day hold, severe at a 1-day hold. Entry at the open on an announcement day means an unusually wide spread.
strategies.shorting_leverage: Short side required for the full effect, and the short side is where the remaining drift concentrates - which is also where borrow is hardest and most expensive. Unverifiable locally.
strategies.redundancy: Distinct from everything the project has already ruled out. Partially overlaps earnings-announcement-premium but that is a different mechanism (attention, not underreaction).
strategies.common_sense: Sensible. Slow incorporation of public information is a well-documented human tendency and the trade direction follows the news direction, so nothing is fighting an obvious interest.
strategies.reason: Longest-surviving anomaly in the literature, mechanism is clear, testable locally if announcement timing exists, and the 60-day variant has tolerable turnover unlike most of this list.

preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes 0.15% round trip on announcement-day entry, 60-day hold, liquid universe only, no short-borrow cost modelled. Long-only version roughly half the return and no borrow problem.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Academic figures of 5-10% are usually gross and often include microcaps. In a liquid universe net of costs I expect the lower half of that range, and less on the long-only version.

tweaks.change: Replace the price-gap surprise with standardised unexpected earnings (SUE) computed from the fundamentals table.
tweaks.why: The gap conflates the surprise with the market's immediate reaction. SUE measures the surprise independently, which is a different definition of the same idea and avoids trading on gaps caused by something other than earnings.
tweaks.disproof: If SUE-sorted portfolios show no drift where gap-sorted ones do, the effect is a price-continuation artefact rather than an information-underreaction effect.

tweaks.change: Condition on low analyst coverage or low institutional ownership.
tweaks.why: Underreaction should be strongest where fewest people are watching. Turns a market-wide claim into a conditional one.
tweaks.disproof: If drift is flat across coverage terciles, limited attention is not the mechanism.

tweaks.change: Trade only the long side.
tweaks.why: Removes the borrow cost and availability problem entirely, which is unverifiable with local data anyway.
tweaks.disproof: If long-only returns are indistinguishable from the market after factor adjustment, the tradeable portion of the effect is on the short side and this strategy is not accessible.

tweaks.change: Extend the hold from 1 day to 20-60 days.
tweaks.why: Cuts turnover several-fold and matches the horizon the literature actually documents.
tweaks.disproof: If cumulative return does not grow with horizon, there is no drift and only a one-day reaction.

strategies.name: Cash flow to market (CF)
strategies.one_line: Rank the universe on the signal; long the cheapest quantile, short the most expensive. Signal: Cash flow to market.
strategies.hypothesis: Stocks that are cheap relative to a fundamental anchor earn higher subsequent returns. Two competing explanations, and the catalogue should not pretend they are settled. The risk story says cheap firms are distressed and the premium compensates for that risk. The behavioural story says investors extrapolate recent poor performance too far and the price overshoots. The two make different predictions about when value fails - the risk story says it fails in bad times, the behavioural story says it fails when extrapolation intensifies - and the 2007-2020 value drawdown is consistent with neither cleanly.
strategies.universe: US common stocks, equal-weighted, with OSAP's stated filter: exchcd%in%c(1,2). Use point-in-time index membership and include delisted names.
strategies.entry_rule: Rank the universe on the signal; long the cheapest quantile, short the most expensive. Signal definition, verbatim from OSAP SignalDoc 2025.10: Net income (ib) plus depreciation (dp) divided by market equity. Exclude NASDAQ stocks.
strategies.exit_rule: Hold 12 month(s), then rebalance into the newly ranked portfolio. Start month 6.0. No stop-loss in the published specification.
strategies.position_sizing: equal-weighted within each leg; long and short legs sized to equal gross exposure. Long-short quantile: 0.1.

strategies.replication_notes: Replicated by the Open Source Asset Pricing project (Chen and Zimmermann), release 2025.10. OSAP replication quality flag: 1_good. Original-paper test: port sort. OSAP evidence summary: t=3.4 in port sort.

claimed_performance.metric: monthly long-short return and t-statistic, as reported in the original paper
claimed_performance.source_note: Author's claim as recorded by OSAP, gross of trading costs. Not a result.

strategies.known_decay: McLean and Pontiff (2016) measure roughly 58% average post-publication decay across 97 predictors; this one was published in 1994, giving it about 32 years of exposure. Hou, Xue and Zhang (2020) fail to replicate the majority of the anomaly literature once microcaps are handled properly and value-weighting is used. Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) argue the significance hurdle should be near t=3.0 rather than 2.0; this signal's original t-statistic is 3.379. Novy-Marx and Velikov (2016) is the direct source for whether this family's gross spread survives its own turnover.
strategies.capacity_notes: Academic long-short spreads of this type are typically measured on a full cross-section including microcaps, where most of the gross spread lives and where a personal account can still trade but an institution cannot. Capacity is not the binding constraint at personal scale; borrow availability on the short leg is.
strategies.data_gap: Requires the specific accounting fields named in the definition. Whether the local fundamentals table carries them is unverified and is the gating question.
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Low - annual rebalancing is the cheapest profile in this catalogue
strategies.shorting_leverage: Short leg required for the published spread. Borrow cost and availability data are unavailable locally, so any short-side edge is unverifiable and must be marked so. A long-only version is testable without that caveat and typically captures under half the spread.
strategies.redundancy: Economic category 'valuation'. Check overlap with other entries in the same category before testing more than one. None of this family overlaps the project's existing negative findings on trend-following, insider transactions, or microcap gap fades.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible on its face: the trade direction follows from the stated mechanism and does not require any participant to act against their own interest.
strategies.reason: Value is among the most crowded factors in finance and suffered a decade-long drawdown from roughly 2007. Test it, but not in its published form.

preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes value-weighting or a liquidity cap rather than equal-weighting, a 0.3% round trip, and no short-borrow cost modelled. I expect roughly a third to a half of the published gross spread to survive: roughly half of the reduction is the microcap and equal-weighting effect that Hou, Xue and Zhang isolate, and the rest is costs plus post-publication crowding.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: The published figure is an equal-weighted gross spread over the original sample. My estimate is lower for three stated reasons: equal-weighting loads the result on microcaps, costs are not deducted, and the sample ends before the post-publication period.

tweaks.change: Value-weight both legs, or cap position size by a liquidity measure, instead of equal-weighting.
tweaks.why: Equal-weighting is where most published anomaly returns come from, and it is the specific choice Hou, Xue and Zhang identify as the reason so many fail to replicate. This tests whether the effect is real or is a microcap artefact.
tweaks.disproof: If the spread vanishes under value-weighting, the anomaly is a microcap artefact and is not worth pursuing further.

tweaks.change: Run the signal only on the post-publication window (publication year to present) as a clean out-of-sample test.
tweaks.why: Directly measures decay rather than assuming it. The local data window is unusually well suited to this, since it begins in 1998 and most of these were published in the 1990s and 2000s.
tweaks.disproof: If the post-publication spread is statistically indistinguishable from zero, the edge is gone and no amount of re-tuning recovers it.

tweaks.change: Test the long leg alone against a matched-beta benchmark.
tweaks.why: Removes the unverifiable short-borrow assumption entirely and produces a number that could actually be traded.
tweaks.disproof: If the long leg alone does not beat its benchmark, the entire effect is on the short side and is not accessible without borrow data.

tweaks.change: Vary the holding period and quantile breakpoint.
tweaks.why: Cheapest way to find out whether the signal decays faster or slower than the published rebalance frequency assumes.
tweaks.disproof: If results are highly sensitive to both, the original specification was fitted and the effect is fragile.

strategies.known_decay: McLean and Pontiff (2016) measure roughly 58% average post-publication decay across 97 predictors; this one was published in 2006, giving it about 20 years of exposure. Hou, Xue and Zhang (2020) fail to replicate the majority of the anomaly literature once microcaps are handled properly and value-weighting is used. Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) argue the significance hurdle should be near t=3.0 rather than 2.0; this signal's original t-statistic is 7.21. Novy-Marx and Velikov (2016) is the direct source for whether this family's gross spread survives its own turnover.
strategies.capacity_notes: Academic long-short spreads of this type are typically measured on a full cross-section including microcaps, where most of the gross spread lives and where a personal account can still trade but an institution cannot. Capacity is not the binding constraint at personal scale; borrow availability on the short leg is.
strategies.cost_sensitivity: High - monthly rebalancing of a full cross-section
strategies.shorting_leverage: Short leg required for the published spread. Borrow cost and availability data are unavailable locally, so any short-side edge is unverifiable and must be marked so. A long-only version is testable without that caveat and typically captures under half the spread.
strategies.redundancy: Economic category 'momentum'. Check overlap with other entries in the same category before testing more than one. None of this family overlaps the project's existing negative findings on trend-following, insider transactions, or microcap gap fades.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible on its face: the trade direction follows from the stated mechanism and does not require any participant to act against their own interest.
strategies.reason: Momentum is heavily crowded and subject to infrequent, severe crashes in post-crisis rebounds. The conditioning variable is the part worth testing, not the raw signal.

preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes value-weighting or a liquidity cap rather than equal-weighting, a 0.3% round trip, and no short-borrow cost modelled. I expect roughly a third to a half of the published gross spread to survive: roughly half of the reduction is the microcap and equal-weighting effect that Hou, Xue and Zhang isolate, and the rest is costs plus post-publication crowding.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: The published figure is an equal-weighted gross spread over the original sample. My estimate is lower for three stated reasons: equal-weighting loads the result on microcaps, costs are not deducted, and the sample ends before the post-publication period.

tweaks.change: Value-weight both legs, or cap position size by a liquidity measure, instead of equal-weighting.
tweaks.why: Equal-weighting is where most published anomaly returns come from, and it is the specific choice Hou, Xue and Zhang identify as the reason so many fail to replicate. This tests whether the effect is real or is a microcap artefact.
tweaks.disproof: If the spread vanishes under value-weighting, the anomaly is a microcap artefact and is not worth pursuing further.

tweaks.change: Run the signal only on the post-publication window (publication year to present) as a clean out-of-sample test.
tweaks.why: Directly measures decay rather than assuming it. The local data window is unusually well suited to this, since it begins in 1998 and most of these were published in the 1990s and 2000s.
tweaks.disproof: If the post-publication spread is statistically indistinguishable from zero, the edge is gone and no amount of re-tuning recovers it.

tweaks.change: Test the long leg alone against a matched-beta benchmark.
tweaks.why: Removes the unverifiable short-borrow assumption entirely and produces a number that could actually be traded.
tweaks.disproof: If the long leg alone does not beat its benchmark, the entire effect is on the short side and is not accessible without borrow data.

tweaks.change: Vary the holding period and quantile breakpoint.
tweaks.why: Cheapest way to find out whether the signal decays faster or slower than the published rebalance frequency assumes.
tweaks.disproof: If results are highly sensitive to both, the original specification was fitted and the effect is fragile.

strategies.name: Investment to revenue (Investment)
strategies.one_line: Rank on the investment or balance-sheet growth measure; long the lowest quantile, short the highest. Signal: Investment to revenue.
strategies.hypothesis: Firms that invest heavily - growing assets, issuing equity, expanding the balance sheet - subsequently underperform. The q-theory explanation is mechanical rather than behavioural: a firm invests when its cost of capital is low, and a low cost of capital is a low expected return. The behavioural explanation is empire-building and overextrapolation by management. The q-theory version is the stronger one because it does not require anyone to be making a mistake.
strategies.universe: US common stocks, value-weighted, with OSAP's stated filter: none stated. Use point-in-time index membership and include delisted names.
strategies.entry_rule: Rank on the investment or balance-sheet growth measure; long the lowest quantile, short the highest. Signal definition, verbatim from OSAP SignalDoc 2025.10: Ratio of capital investment (capx) to revenue (revt) divided by the firm-specific 36-month rolling mean of that ratio. Exclude if revenue less than \$10m.
strategies.exit_rule: Hold 12 month(s), then rebalance into the newly ranked portfolio. Start month 6.0. No stop-loss in the published specification.
strategies.position_sizing: value-weighted within each leg; long and short legs sized to equal gross exposure. Long-short quantile: 0.2.

strategies.name: Share issuance (5 year) (ShareIss5Y)
strategies.one_line: Rank on net share issuance over the measurement window; long net repurchasers, short net issuers. Signal: Share issuance (5 year).
strategies.hypothesis: Firms that issue shares underperform and firms that repurchase outperform. Management has better information about the firm's value than outside investors and issues when the stock is expensive. This is one of the few anomalies with a mechanism that is difficult to argue away, because it rests on an information asymmetry that is structural to the corporate form rather than on an investor error.

strategies.known_decay: McLean and Pontiff (2016) measure roughly 58% average post-publication decay across 97 predictors; this one was published in 1996, giving it about 30 years of exposure. strategies.name: Pastor-Stambaugh liquidity beta (BetaLiquidityPS)
strategies.one_line: Estimate each stock's loading on an aggregate liquidity innovation series; long high loadings, short low. Signal: Pastor-Stambaugh liquidity beta.
strategies.hypothesis: Stocks whose returns are most sensitive to market-wide liquidity shocks earn a premium, because they are worst to hold precisely when liquidity dries up and an investor most wants to sell. This is a genuine risk premium rather than a mispricing, which means it should not decay with publication - and equally means it should be expected to deliver its worst losses at the worst possible moment.
strategies.universe: US common stocks, value-weighted, with OSAP's stated filter: abs(prc)>5. Use point-in-time index membership and include delisted names.
strategies.entry_rule: Estimate each stock's loading on an aggregate liquidity innovation series; long high loadings, short low. Signal definition, verbatim from OSAP SignalDoc 2025.10: Monthly excess return (ret -rf) regressed on innovations in liquidity from Pastor's website (\url{https://faculty.chicagobooth.edu/lubos.pastor/research/liq_data_1962_2018.txt}). Use 60 month rolling window regression, and require at least 36 non-missing observations.

strategies.name: Futures Carry (Carver Strategy 10)
strategies.one_line: Hold long futures whose nearer contract is priced above the farther one, short those where it is below, sized by how steep that slope is relative to the instrument's volatility.
strategies.hypothesis: The futures curve slope is a direct estimate of the return earned from the passage of time if the spot price does not move. In backwardation the near contract is dearer than the far one, so rolling forward earns the difference; in contango it loses it. The economic content is that the slope compensates someone for holding a risk - the physical inventory for commodities, the currency differential for FX, the equity risk premium net of financing for stock indices. Carry is therefore not a forecast of price direction; it is payment for standing on the unpopular side of a hedging imbalance. That is why it is uncorrelated with trend and why it keeps working despite being obvious: the imbalance does not go away.
strategies.universe: A diversified set of liquid futures across asset classes - equity indices, bonds, FX, commodities. Carver's own portfolios span 30-100 instruments; a small account can run 8-15.
strategies.entry_rule: For each instrument compute raw carry = (price of nearer contract - price of farther contract) annualised by the fraction of a year between their expiries. Divide by the instrument's annualised price volatility to get a risk-adjusted carry. Scale into a forecast capped at a fixed maximum. Go long where the forecast is positive, short where negative, proportional to forecast strength.
strategies.exit_rule: No discrete exit. The position is continuously re-sized as carry and volatility change, and flips sign when carry flips. Positions are rolled before expiry on a fixed schedule.
strategies.position_sizing: Volatility targeting: position = (capital * risk_target * forecast) / (instrument volatility * contract value). Carver's default annualised risk target is in the 20-25% range for a diversified portfolio and should be reduced for a concentrated one.
strategies.rebalance_frequency: daily re-sizing with a no-trade buffer to suppress churn

strategies.name: Trend Following with EWMAC Filters (Carver Strategies 7-9)
strategies.one_line: Go long or short each futures instrument according to the sign and strength of the gap between a fast and a slow exponentially weighted moving average, sized by volatility.
strategies.hypothesis: Prices trend because information is incorporated gradually and because some participants systematically add to positions as prices move - hedgers adjusting, risk-parity funds rebalancing, stop-losses triggering. The trend follower is paid to absorb the resulting flow. The payoff profile is intrinsically option-like: many small losses in choppy markets, a few large gains in sustained moves. This matters because the mechanism predicts the shape of the return distribution, not just its mean, and any test that looks only at the mean will misjudge it.
strategies.universe: Diversified liquid futures across equity indices, bonds, FX and commodities.
strategies.entry_rule: For each instrument and each speed pair (N, 4N) with N in {2,4,8,16,32,64}: compute EWMAC = EWMA(N) - EWMA(4N) of the price. Divide by the instrument's price volatility to make it comparable across instruments, then scale to a common forecast scale and cap it. Combine the speeds into a single forecast using a weighted average with a diversification multiplier. Position sign follows the combined forecast sign.
strategies.exit_rule: No discrete exit. Position size is continuous in the forecast and reverses when the forecast changes sign. Contracts are rolled on a fixed schedule before expiry.
strategies.position_sizing: Volatility targeting identical to the carry strategy: position scales with forecast strength and inversely with instrument volatility, to a portfolio-level annualised risk target.

strategies.name: Crypto Spot-Perpetual Basis (Funding Rate Carry)
strategies.one_line: Hold spot crypto and short the same amount of the perpetual future, collecting the funding payment while carrying no price exposure.
strategies.hypothesis: Perpetual futures have no expiry, so the exchange forces convergence to spot by making one side pay the other a funding rate every interval. When retail demand for leveraged long exposure exceeds short demand - which is most of the time in crypto bull markets - the perpetual trades above spot and longs pay shorts. A trader who is long spot and short perp has no directional exposure and collects that payment. The mechanism is explicit, mechanical and published by each exchange; it is not a statistical pattern. What is being harvested is retail leverage demand, and it persists because that demand persists.
strategies.universe: Major pairs with deep perpetual markets - BTC and ETH first, then large-cap alts. Restricted to exchanges a US person can legally access, which is the binding constraint.
strategies.entry_rule: Compute the annualised funding rate as the realised funding per interval times the number of intervals per year (three 8-hour intervals daily on Binance, Bybit and OKX, so 1095 per year). Enter a delta-neutral position - long spot, short perpetual of equal notional - when the trailing 30-day mean annualised funding exceeds a threshold, with 10% a reasonable starting point. Size legs to equal notional, not equal contract count.
strategies.exit_rule: Close both legs when trailing funding falls below the threshold, or immediately on any of: exchange withdrawal suspension, a funding rate sign flip persisting more than three intervals, or margin ratio on the short leg falling below a preset floor.
strategies.position_sizing: Equal notional on both legs. Short-perp margin must be over-collateralised well beyond the exchange minimum, because a sharp rally raises the mark price and can liquidate the short leg even though the combined position is flat. Carver-style volatility targeting is inappropriate here; the risk is discrete and operational, not continuous.
strategies.rebalance_frequency: daily delta re-hedge; funding settles every 8 hours

strategies.name: Event Contract Internal No-Arbitrage (Yes + No Below $1)
strategies.one_line: When the yes and no contracts on the same event together cost less than a dollar, buy both and collect the guaranteed dollar at settlement.
strategies.hypothesis: A yes contract and a no contract on the same binary event pay exactly one dollar between them in every state of the world. If their combined ask price is below a dollar the position is a riskless claim bought at a discount. No forecasting is involved and no view on the event is required. Violations arise from thin books, stale quotes on one side, and the fact that most participants trade one side only and never look at the pair.
strategies.universe: All Kalshi binary markets; the same structure exists on Polymarket. In practice only markets with two-sided quotes on both legs are tradeable.
strategies.entry_rule: Continuously monitor the best ask on yes (Py) and the best ask on no (Pn) for the same contract. Compute gross edge = 1 - (Py + Pn). Compute the fee: for taker execution on Kalshi, 0.07*Py*(1-Py) + 0.07*Pn*(1-Pn) per contract pair. Enter both legs simultaneously only when gross edge exceeds that fee by a margin covering slippage.
strategies.exit_rule: Hold both legs to settlement. There is no exit decision; the pair self-liquidates at one dollar.
strategies.position_sizing: Limited by the smaller of the two legs' available depth at the quoted price. Capital consumed is (Py + Pn) per pair, locked until resolution.

strategies.capital_required: Capital is consumed at roughly the full dollar of eventual payout per pair, and is locked from entry until resolution. Pre-positioning is required: funds must already sit in the Kalshi account when the violation appears, because a transfer takes far longer than the opportunity lasts. Practical minimum to operate is a few thousand dollars of idle balance, and that idle balance is a real cost that most analyses of this trade ignore.
strategies.fee_model: Kalshi, per its published fee schedule (July 2026 revision): fees = roundup(0.07 x C x P x (1-P)) for takers; roundup(0.0175 x C x P x (1-P)) for makers on eligible series; roundup(0.035 x C x P x (1-P)) for S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 series. There is no settlement fee. Polymarket: fee = C x feeRate x p x (1-p), with makers charged zero across all categories and taker rates of 0.07 crypto, 0.05 sports/economics/culture/weather, 0.04 finance/politics/tech, and 0.00 geopolitics. No deposit or withdrawal fee on either venue, though on-chain gas and stablecoin conversion apply to Polymarket.
strategies.net_edge_analysis: THE FEE IS QUADRATIC IN PRICE AND THIS DETERMINES EVERYTHING. Combined taker fee on the pair is approximately 0.14*p*(1-p), which is maximised at p=0.50 and falls sharply toward the extremes. Break-even combined price, taker execution: p=0.50 requires Py+Pn below $0.9650; p=0.35 below $0.9681; p=0.20 below $0.9776; p=0.10 below $0.9874; p=0.05 below $0.9933; p=0.02 below $0.9973. A 3.5-cent gap on a coin-flip contract essentially never appears in a market with any participation at all, so THE TRADE DOES NOT EXIST NEAR 50 CENTS. It exists, if anywhere, on far-from-even contracts where the required gap falls under a cent. Maker execution changes the picture materially: the maker rate of 0.0175 cuts the fee fourfold, moving break-even at p=0.50 to $0.9912 and at p=0.05 to $0.9983 - but resting orders are not guaranteed to fill, which converts a riskless arbitrage into a one-legged directional position when only one side executes.
strategies.return_per_capital_per_day: Dominated by time to resolution, not by edge size. For a 1-cent net edge on approximately $1 of locked capital: 52.7% annualised if the contract resolves in 7 days, 26.3% at 14 days, 12.3% at 30 days, 4.1% at 90 days, 2.0% at 180 days. A 0.5-cent edge at 7 days (26.2% annualised) beats a 3-cent edge at 180 days (6.3%). The correct screen is therefore short-dated contracts in the price tails, and long-dated political markets - where retail attention concentrates - are the worst place to look.
strategies.execution_risk: The dominant risk. If the yes leg fills and the no leg does not, the position is an outright directional bet acquired at a price chosen for arbitrage reasons rather than for any view. Both legs must be submitted as immediate-or-cancel and any partial fill unwound at once, accepting the loss. Because the edge is under a cent, a single unhedged leg can erase many successful trades. This is why the strategy's realistic expectancy is far below its gross arithmetic.
strategies.latency_note: Not sub-second. Violations in thin markets persist for minutes because there are few automated participants in the long tail of Kalshi's market list. This is the specific reason the strategy is not automatically disqualified under the co-location rule.
strategies.reason: Genuinely riskless payoff structure, latency requirements a person at a laptop can meet, and exact rather than estimated fee math - but it must start with data recording today, because settled market history is purged and cannot be recovered later.

strategies.name: Event Contract Mutually Exclusive Overround
strategies.one_line: When the yes prices of all mutually exclusive outcomes of one event sum above a dollar, sell every outcome and keep the excess.
strategies.hypothesis: Exactly one of a set of mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive outcomes must occur, so their yes contracts must sum to one dollar. If they sum above a dollar, selling all of them collects more than the single dollar that will be paid out. Overrounds arise in multi-outcome markets - election fields, sports brackets, economic data buckets - because participants price each leg independently against its own narrative and nobody enforces the cross-leg constraint.
strategies.universe: Kalshi multi-outcome market groups where the outcome set is genuinely exhaustive and mutually exclusive. Verifying exhaustiveness from the contract terms is the critical and easily-botched step.
strategies.entry_rule: For a group of N mutually exclusive outcomes, compute S = sum of best bid prices across all legs. Compute the total fee 0.07 * sum over i of p_i*(1-p_i). Enter short on all N legs simultaneously only when S - 1 exceeds that total fee plus a slippage margin.
strategies.exit_rule: Hold all legs to settlement. Exactly one pays out one dollar; the rest expire worthless.
strategies.position_sizing: Equal contract count across every leg. Collateral requirement is the full payout on the winning leg, so capital consumed is approximately one dollar per set.

strategies.name: Closed-End Fund Discount Mean Reversion
strategies.one_line: Buy closed-end funds trading at unusually wide discounts to their net asset value and sell as the discount narrows toward its own norm.
strategies.hypothesis: A closed-end fund has a fixed share count, so its market price can diverge from the value of the assets it holds. The discount is not itself an anomaly - it reflects fees, illiquidity and tax overhangs - but the variation in the discount around each fund's own long-run level is mean-reverting. The mechanism is sentiment-driven retail flow into and out of a fixed supply, and it is bounded by the fact that a persistent extreme discount eventually attracts activist pressure or a tender offer, which forces convergence. The trade is on the deviation, not on the level.
strategies.universe: US-listed closed-end funds with daily or weekly published NAV, adequate trading volume, and at least three years of discount history for computing a baseline.
strategies.entry_rule: For each fund compute discount = (price - NAV) / NAV. Compute its z-score against that fund's own trailing 1-year mean and standard deviation of discount. Buy when the z-score falls below -1.5. Optionally hedge the asset-class exposure with a matching index ETF short to isolate the discount.
strategies.exit_rule: Exit when the z-score returns above -0.25, or after 6 months without convergence, or immediately on a distribution cut or a change in fund mandate.
strategies.position_sizing: Equal weight across qualifying funds, capped by a per-fund liquidity limit of a small fraction of average daily volume.

Sources: CEFConnect publishes current and some historical data but does not offer bulk download; Morningstar Direct and Refinitiv carry full history at institutional pricing. Retail-accessible bulk NAV history is genuinely hard to obtain and this is the single obstacle to testing.
strategies.turnover: Moderate - positions held weeks to months
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Moderate to high. CEF spreads are wide relative to common stocks, often 0.3-1.0%, which consumes a meaningful share of a convergence trade sized in single-digit percentage points.
strategies.shorting_leverage: The optional index hedge requires a short ETF position, which is straightforward and cheap to borrow. No hard-to-borrow problem.
strategies.redundancy: No overlap with the project's prior findings or with the rest of the catalogue.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible. The convergence mechanism is real and enforced by an identifiable participant - activist investors with a profit motive to close the gap.
strategies.arb_type_justification: Not riskless. Nothing forces a discount to close on any timetable, and discounts can widen for years. The bound is soft and enforced only by the possibility of activist intervention, which may not come.
strategies.capital_required: No pre-positioning beyond a normal brokerage balance. Capital is tied up for the holding period.
strategies.fee_model: Standard US equity commissions, effectively zero at most retail brokers. The real cost is the bid-ask spread on thin CEFs, which is 0.3-1.0% round trip and must be modelled explicitly rather than assumed away.
strategies.net_edge_analysis: A 2-standard-deviation discount widening on a fund whose discount normally sits at 8% with a 3-point standard deviation represents roughly 6 points of potential convergence. Against a 0.5-1.0% round-trip spread the gross-to-net ratio is favourable, unlike most entries in this catalogue. The binding question is not fees but how often convergence actually occurs within the holding window.
strategies.return_per_capital_per_day: A 4-point convergence realised over 90 days on fully committed capital is roughly 16% annualised on the position, before accounting for the trades that do not converge. Portfolio-level returns will be a fraction of this.
strategies.execution_risk: Low for the unhedged version. The hedged version carries basis risk between the fund's actual holdings and the index used to hedge, which can exceed the discount convergence being harvested.
strategies.latency_note: Discounts move over days and weeks. Entirely compatible with a person at a laptop.
strategies.reason: Good mechanism with a real enforcement channel and a favourable cost-to-edge ratio, but historical NAV data is not held locally and is not cheaply obtainable, which blocks any test.

preliminary_estimate.expected_drawdown: 15-25%; discounts widen hardest in exactly the drawdowns where everything else is also falling
preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes 0.7% round-trip spread, unhedged, liquid CEFs only. The correlation of discount widening with general market stress means this diversifies less than it appears to.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Practitioner mid-single-digit claims are plausible but rest on thinner evidence than the academic entries here, and typically do not model CEF spreads honestly.

tweaks.change: Restrict to funds where an activist holder has filed a 13D, which is available in the local data.
tweaks.why: The convergence mechanism is activist pressure; conditioning on its actual presence turns a hope into an identified catalyst. This is a genuine change of the idea, and it uses data already held.
tweaks.disproof: If convergence rates are no higher in funds with activist filings, activism is not the enforcement channel and the mechanism story is wrong.

tweaks.change: Hedge with the fund's actual disclosed holdings rather than a proxy index.
tweaks.why: Removes the basis risk that can exceed the edge. Requires N-PORT parsing.
tweaks.disproof: If hedged returns are no less volatile than unhedged, the asset exposure was not the dominant risk and the hedge is wasted cost.

tweaks.change: Add a distribution-coverage filter, excluding funds paying distributions from return of capital.
tweaks.why: Wide discounts frequently signal an unsustainable distribution about to be cut, which is a value trap rather than a mispricing.
tweaks.disproof: If excluded funds converge as often as included ones, distribution sustainability is not what distinguishes a trap.

tweaks.disproof: Strong sensitivity means fragility.

strategies.name: G10 Currency Carry
strategies.one_line: Go long the currencies with the highest short-term interest rates and short those with the lowest, rebalancing monthly.
strategies.hypothesis: Uncovered interest parity says a high-yielding currency should depreciate by exactly its rate advantage, leaving no profit. Empirically it does not, and often appreciates instead. The premium is usually explained as compensation for crash risk: carry produces small steady gains punctuated by violent unwinds when risk appetite collapses and leveraged positions are liquidated simultaneously. The mechanism is real but the compensation is for a risk that shows up rarely and all at once, which makes standard risk statistics systematically flatter it.
strategies.universe: G10 currencies against USD: AUD, CAD, CHF, EUR, GBP, JPY, NOK, NZD, SEK.
strategies.entry_rule: Each month rank the nine currencies by their short-term interest rate differential against USD, proxied by 3-month forward points. Go long the top three, short the bottom three, in equal notional.
strategies.exit_rule: Rebalance monthly into the newly ranked portfolio. No stop-loss in the published specification, which is a material weakness given the crash profile.
strategies.position_sizing: Equal notional per currency, optionally scaled inversely to trailing FX volatility.

claimed_performance.source_note: Author's claim, gross. Critically, these figures are computed on a sample that includes the 2008 unwind; figures quoted from samples ending before 2008 are far higher and should be distrusted.

strategies.known_decay: G10 rate differentials compressed to near zero through the 2010s zero-rate era, which removed most of the raw signal. The premium requires dispersion in policy rates to exist at all, and for roughly a decade there was none. Rate dispersion returned after 2022, so the strategy is arguably more viable now than at any point since 2008 - but that is a regime observation, not evidence.
strategies.capacity_notes: Very large. FX is the deepest market in the world and capacity is not a constraint at any personal scale.
strategies.data_gap: FX spot and forward history is not held locally. Broker feeds (Interactive Brokers, OANDA) provide spot history free with an account; clean forward-points history is harder and typically requires a paid feed or careful construction from deposit rates. Estimated cost: low if built from free central bank rate data, moderate if bought.
strategies.turnover: Low - monthly rebalancing of nine currencies
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Low. FX spreads on G10 pairs are among the tightest in any market, and monthly turnover on nine instruments is trivial.
strategies.shorting_leverage: Symmetric; no borrow constraint. Leverage is available and cheap, which is precisely what makes the crash risk dangerous.
strategies.redundancy: Diversifies the equity-heavy catalogue. Correlated with other carry entries, particularly futures carry, since both harvest the same cross-asset premium.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible, with a caveat worth stating plainly: the trade is structurally short a tail risk. The steady profits are the premium and the occasional violent loss is the thing being insured against. Any evaluation that treats the crash as an outlier to be excluded has misunderstood the strategy.
strategies.reason: Strong mechanism, near-zero cost sensitivity, and genuine diversification - but it needs FX data not held locally, and its payoff profile makes it a poor fit for an account that cannot tolerate a sudden 20% loss.

preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes post-2022 rate dispersion persists, unlevered, G10 only. I discount academic figures because the strongest sample period preceded 2008.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Published Sharpes of 0.4-0.7 mostly predate the zero-rate decade during which the strategy had essentially no signal. I estimate the lower end.

tweaks.disproof: If filtered returns fall as much as filtered volatility, the crash risk is the premium and cannot be hedged away without destroying the trade.

tweaks.disproof: If EM carry returns are fully explained by EM equity beta, it is not a distinct premium.

strategies.name: Volatility Risk Premium (Systematic Short Straddle or Strangle)
strategies.one_line: Sell index options and hold to expiry, collecting the persistent gap between implied and subsequently realised volatility.
strategies.hypothesis: Implied volatility on index options exceeds subsequently realised volatility most of the time. The standard explanation is that index options are insurance: investors pay a premium above fair value for downside protection because the payoff arrives precisely when everything else they own is falling. The seller earns that premium for bearing the risk. This is a genuine risk premium with an identifiable buyer and an identifiable motive, which is why it persists despite being universally known - but for exactly the same reason, the losses are severe and arrive without warning.
strategies.universe: Liquid index options: SPX, or SPY for smaller size. Single-name options have a much less reliable premium and far worse liquidity.
strategies.entry_rule: At a fixed monthly interval sell a delta-neutral straddle or a 15-delta strangle on the index, 30-45 days to expiry. Optionally condition entry on the VIX term structure being in contango, which indicates the premium is present.
strategies.exit_rule: Hold to expiry, or close at 50% of maximum profit, or close on a stop at 2x credit received. Roll to the next expiry.
strategies.position_sizing: Position size must be set by the loss at a defined tail move, not by premium collected or by margin. Sizing on margin is how this strategy destroys accounts, because margin requirements understate the tail.
strategies.rebalance_frequency: monthly, with optional delta re-hedging between rolls

strategies.replication_notes: Cboe publishes the BXM (buy-write) and PUT (put-write) indices as long-running investable benchmarks for this premium, which is unusually good evidence by the standards of this catalogue - it is a live index rather than a backtest. Euan Sinclair's 'Volatility Trading', in the local reference folder, is the practitioner treatment and is notably more sober about costs than most sources.

claimed_performance.metric: risk-adjusted return
claimed_performance.value: Cboe's PUT and BXM indices have historically shown returns comparable to the S&P 500 at meaningfully lower volatility. Malkiel et al. report improved risk-adjusted returns from VIX-conditioned option writing.
claimed_performance.source_note: Cboe is the exchange that lists the options, which is a conflict worth naming. The indices are nonetheless real published series rather than a private backtest.

strategies.known_decay: The premium has compressed as volatility selling became a retail product. The February 2018 and March 2020 episodes both produced catastrophic losses for levered short-volatility vehicles, including the complete destruction of at least one listed ETP. Compression of the premium plus unchanged tail risk is the worst possible combination.
strategies.capacity_notes: Large in SPX. Not a constraint at personal scale.
strategies.data_gap: Option chain history is not entitled locally. OptionMetrics IvyDB is the academic standard at institutional pricing; CBOE DataShop sells historical option data at roughly $500-2000 for a meaningful SPX history; ORATS and Polygon offer cheaper retail options data from roughly $50-200/month. This is purchasable at retail cost, unlike most of the blocked entries here.
strategies.cost_sensitivity: High. Option bid-ask spreads are wide relative to the premium collected, and the strategy is short an asset whose spread widens exactly when it is most needed to close.
strategies.shorting_leverage: Short options carry undefined risk on the straddle version and require margin. Defined-risk variants - iron condors, credit spreads - cap the loss at a known cost in premium and are the only version appropriate for an account that cannot absorb a tail event.
strategies.redundancy: No overlap with anything else in the catalogue.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible, and the common-sense test is instructive here. This strategy does not fight an obvious interest - the buyer of index puts wants insurance and knowingly pays above fair value for it. But it does require the seller to be able to survive the event being insured against, and that is a balance-sheet question, not a signal question.
strategies.reason: The premium is real and unusually well evidenced, but it cannot be validated on local data, and more importantly its risk is a fat left tail that no backtest on a short sample will reveal. It should be evaluated by hand on a small defined-risk forward sample rather than backtested into false confidence.

preliminary_estimate.expected_annual_return_over_bh: 0-4% over buy-and-hold in normal years, with occasional single-year losses exceeding 30%
preliminary_estimate.rough_sharpe: 0.5-0.9 measured conventionally, which materially overstates the attractiveness because Sharpe does not price a fat left tail
preliminary_estimate.expected_drawdown: 40%+ in a volatility shock; higher with any leverage
preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes defined-risk structures, no leverage, retail option spreads. The Sharpe figure should be treated as misleading rather than informative for this entry.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Cboe index figures are computed without transaction costs and on an unlevered basis. Retail implementation faces wide spreads and the temptation to lever, which is what turns a modest premium into a ruin risk.

tweaks.change: Trade only defined-risk structures - iron condors or credit spreads - never naked straddles.
tweaks.why: Caps the loss at a known amount. Sacrifices premium for survivability, which is the correct trade for an account that cannot absorb a tail.
tweaks.disproof: If defined-risk net returns after the wider spreads of a four-leg structure are indistinguishable from zero, the premium does not survive the cost of capping the tail.

tweaks.change: Condition entry on the VIX futures term structure being in contango and stand aside in backwardation.
tweaks.why: Backwardation signals that the market is already in a volatility event, which is exactly when short volatility loses. This targets the loss mechanism directly.
tweaks.disproof: If returns in backwardation months are not materially worse, the term structure carries no regime information.

tweaks.change: Sell volatility on an index while buying it on single names (dispersion).
tweaks.why: Harvests the correlation premium rather than the level of volatility, and is far less directionally exposed to a market shock. A different idea using the same instruments.
tweaks.disproof: If the implied correlation spread does not cover the substantially higher transaction costs of trading many single-name options, dispersion is uneconomic at retail size.

strategies.name: ADR versus Ordinary Share Parity
strategies.one_line: Trade the gap when an American Depositary Receipt diverges from its underlying foreign share price converted at the current exchange rate.
strategies.hypothesis: An ADR is a claim on a fixed number of foreign ordinary shares, so its dollar price should equal the ordinary price times the ratio times the exchange rate. Deviations arise from non-overlapping trading hours, conversion friction and short-term local demand. For ADRs that are freely convertible, a large deviation is bounded by the ability of an authorised participant to create or cancel receipts.
strategies.universe: Liquid ADRs with a freely convertible structure and a liquid ordinary listing in a market with at least partial overlap with US hours - European listings overlap; Asian listings do not.
strategies.entry_rule: Compute parity = ordinary price x ADR ratio x FX rate. Compute deviation = (ADR price - parity) / parity. Enter long ADR / short ordinary when deviation is below a threshold, or the reverse when above, with the threshold set above round-trip costs plus FX conversion.
strategies.exit_rule: Exit on convergence to within a fraction of the entry threshold, or after a fixed maximum holding period.
strategies.position_sizing: Equal notional on both legs, FX-hedged. Size limited by the thinner of the two listings.
strategies.rebalance_frequency: intraday monitoring during the overlap window

strategies.replication_notes: Gagnon and Karolyi document deviations across a large sample of cross-listed pairs and find they are usually small but occasionally large and persistent.

claimed_performance.metric: deviation magnitude
claimed_performance.value: Gagnon and Karolyi find average absolute deviations of a few tens of basis points with a long tail of much larger ones
claimed_performance.source_note: Author's finding about the size of deviations, not a claim about a tradeable strategy's return. The distinction matters - documenting a deviation is not the same as documenting a profit.

strategies.known_decay: The paper's sample ends in 2004 and cross-market electronic trading has improved substantially since. Expect materially smaller deviations now.
strategies.capacity_notes: Small to moderate, limited by the ordinary-share leg and by FX conversion size.
strategies.data_gap: Requires synchronised intraday prices on two exchanges plus intraday FX. Local data is US daily bars only. Intraday international equity data is expensive; realistic sources are Refinitiv or Bloomberg at institutional pricing, or a broker feed recorded forward.
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Decisive. Two equity legs in different currencies plus an FX conversion means three round-trip costs against a gross edge measured in tens of basis points.
strategies.shorting_leverage: Requires shorting the ordinary share in a foreign market, which has its own borrow constraints, settlement conventions and in some jurisdictions regulatory restrictions.
strategies.redundancy: No overlap.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible in principle. The bound is real and enforced by conversion. But the practical question is whether a retail participant can execute a three-legged cross-border trade at a cost below the deviation, and the answer is probably not.
strategies.arb_type_justification: Not riskless for a retail participant. True riskless execution requires the ability to convert receipts, which is restricted to authorised participants. Everyone else is trading a spread that usually converges, which is a statistical bet.

venues.venue: European or Asian exchange for the ordinary
venues.us_retail_accessible: Partially - requires a broker with foreign market access, typically Interactive Brokers, plus FX conversion.

strategies.capital_required: Capital must be pre-positioned in two currencies across two market accounts, which is a substantial hidden cost and a meaningful operational burden.
strategies.fee_model: US leg: effectively zero commission, spread only. Foreign leg: commissions typically 0.05-0.15% plus local stamp duty where applicable (UK 0.5% on purchases, which alone kills the trade for UK ordinaries). FX conversion at Interactive Brokers is roughly 0.002% plus a minimum ticket charge; at most other retail brokers it is 0.5-1.5%, which is fatal. ADR issuers also levy a pass-through fee of typically $0.01-0.05 per share annually.
strategies.net_edge_analysis: Typical deviations of 20-40 basis points against combined costs of roughly 15-30 basis points at the best available retail execution leave little or nothing. With a retail broker's standard FX spread rather than Interactive Brokers' rate, the trade is deeply negative. UK ordinaries are disqualified outright by stamp duty.
strategies.return_per_capital_per_day: Marginal at best, and requires capital idle in two currencies.
strategies.execution_risk: High. The two legs trade in different venues with different hours and settlement cycles. A fill on one leg without the other leaves an unhedged position across a currency boundary.
strategies.latency_note: Deviations during the overlap window persist for minutes, not milliseconds - but the cost structure, not latency, is what disqualifies this.
strategies.reason: Gross deviations are of the same order as realistic retail execution costs, and the trade additionally requires pre-positioned capital in two currencies and foreign short-selling access. It is a real arbitrage for an authorised participant and negative expectancy for everyone else.

preliminary_estimate.expected_annual_return_over_bh: Approximately zero to negative after realistic costs
preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Retail execution, Interactive Brokers FX rates, excluding stamp-duty jurisdictions.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Gagnon and Karolyi document deviation sizes, not net returns. Reading their deviation statistics as a profit opportunity is the error this entry exists to prevent.

strategies.name: Event Contract Narrative Overpricing Fade
strategies.one_line: Systematically sell event contracts on outcomes that are dramatic and emotionally salient but statistically unlikely.
strategies.hypothesis: This is the favourite-longshot bias, one of the oldest documented regularities in betting markets: low-probability outcomes trade above their true frequency and high-probability outcomes below. In event contract markets the proposed mechanism is that casual participants buy a story rather than a probability, and compelling underdog narratives attract disproportionate demand into a market with limited professional capital to absorb it. A systematic seller of salient longshots harvests the bias without needing any view on the specific event.
strategies.universe: Kalshi contracts priced below roughly 15 cents in categories with heavy retail participation - sports, entertainment, high-profile political outcomes. Explicitly excludes economic data releases, where participants are more sophisticated.
strategies.entry_rule: Sell yes contracts priced between 3 and 15 cents in qualifying categories, where a base-rate estimate built from historical frequencies of comparable events is materially below the market price. Require the gap to exceed fees plus a margin.
strategies.exit_rule: Hold to settlement. Optionally close early if the price falls below a third of entry.
strategies.position_sizing: Strictly capped per contract and per correlated group. A portfolio of short longshots has a return profile identical to selling insurance: many small wins and occasional large correlated losses when a single event resolves several positions against the seller at once.

strategies.replication_notes: The favourite-longshot bias is extensively documented in horse racing and sports betting markets over many decades. Whether it transfers at the same magnitude to CFTC-regulated event contracts with a different participant mix is genuinely unestablished and should not be assumed.

claimed_performance.metric: bias magnitude
claimed_performance.value: Racetrack studies typically find longshots at odds beyond 20-to-1 return substantially less than their implied probability. No figure specific to Kalshi located.
claimed_performance.source_note: Author's finding in a different market. Transferring it to event contracts is an assumption, not evidence.

strategies.known_decay: Unknown in this venue. Kalshi's participant mix has professionalised substantially since 2023, which should reduce the bias.
strategies.capacity_notes: Small. Longshot contracts are thin by nature.
strategies.data_gap: PERISHABLE AND URGENT. Kalshi purges settled markets. Testing whether the bias exists on this venue requires a history of settled prices and outcomes which is being destroyed continuously. This is the strongest argument in the entire catalogue for starting a recording process immediately, independent of whether any strategy is ever traded.
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Favourable relative to the other event contract entries. The Kalshi fee of 0.07*p*(1-p) at p=0.10 is 0.63 cents, small against a hypothesised several-point mispricing. This is the one event contract strategy where the quadratic fee works in the trader's favour, because it operates in the price tail.
strategies.shorting_leverage: Selling yes is equivalent to buying no; no borrow. Full collateral is posted, so there is no leverage and no liquidation risk.
strategies.redundancy: No overlap. Distinct from the no-arbitrage entries, which require no view; this one requires a base rate and is therefore a forecasting strategy in disguise.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible but requires care. The mechanism - people paying for stories - is well documented in adjacent markets. The danger is that 'the market is overpricing this longshot' and 'the market knows something I do not' are indistinguishable without a genuine base rate, and constructing that base rate is the entire difficulty.
strategies.arb_type_justification: Not an arbitrage in any sense. It is a forecasting edge based on a claimed population-level bias, with all the estimation risk that implies.
strategies.capital_required: Full collateral on each short position, locked until settlement. A diversified book of 30 positions at 2% each requires the majority of capital committed and idle.
strategies.fee_model: Kalshi taker: roundup(0.07 x C x P x (1-P)). At p=0.10 this is 0.63 cents per contract; at p=0.05, 0.33 cents. Maker execution at 0.0175 reduces this fourfold.
strategies.net_edge_analysis: A hypothesised 3-point overpricing on a contract trading at 10 cents is a 3-cent gross edge against a 0.63-cent fee - the most favourable gross-to-fee ratio of any event contract entry here. The problem is not the fee, it is establishing that the 3-point overpricing is real rather than an artefact of a badly constructed base rate.
strategies.return_per_capital_per_day: A 2.4-cent net edge on roughly 10 cents of collateral is a 24% return on committed capital per event. At a 30-day average resolution that is high in annualised terms, but capital is fully committed and the loss distribution is highly skewed, so the arithmetic flatters it.
strategies.execution_risk: Low - single-leg positions with no hedge to miss.
strategies.latency_note: No speed requirement whatsoever. Entirely compatible with a person at a laptop.
strategies.reason: Cannot be backtested because the venue's history is purged, and it depends on a base-rate estimate that is the hard part and is domain-specific. It should be run as a tracked forward experiment at minimal size, not as a systematic strategy, until a recorded sample exists.

preliminary_estimate.expected_annual_return_over_bh: Unknown. Could plausibly be 5-15% on committed capital if the bias transfers at racetrack magnitudes; could equally be negative if it does not.
preliminary_estimate.rough_sharpe: Unestimable without venue data, and Sharpe is the wrong statistic for a short-insurance payoff anyway
preliminary_estimate.expected_drawdown: Potentially severe and correlated - a single dramatic event can resolve many positions against the seller simultaneously
preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes the racetrack bias transfers to a CFTC-regulated venue with a partly professional participant base. That assumption is doing all the work and is unverified.

strategies.name: Cross-Venue Event Contract Pricing (Kalshi versus Polymarket)
strategies.one_line: Buy the cheaper side of the same real-world outcome on one venue and sell it on the other when the two disagree by more than the combined fees.
strategies.hypothesis: Kalshi and Polymarket list contracts on many of the same events - elections, macroeconomic releases, major sporting outcomes. Because the two venues have almost entirely separate participant bases, separate collateral (USD versus USDC), and separate regulatory status, capital does not flow freely between them and prices can diverge persistently. The divergence is not an inefficiency in the usual sense; it is the price of the friction between two segmented pools.
strategies.universe: Event pairs where both venues list a contract on an outcome with identical resolution criteria. Verifying that the resolution criteria genuinely match is the critical step and the most common source of error.
strategies.entry_rule: For matched contracts compute the price difference net of each venue's fee. Buy on the cheaper venue and sell the equivalent exposure on the dearer one when the net difference exceeds a threshold covering both fees plus a margin for resolution-criteria risk.
strategies.exit_rule: Hold both legs to settlement, provided resolution criteria are genuinely identical. If they are not, the position is not hedged and must be managed directionally.
strategies.position_sizing: Limited by the thinner venue and by capital pre-positioned on both.
