published.title: Cross-venue price divergence under segmented capital

strategies.replication_notes: Divergences between the two venues were widely reported during the 2024 US election cycle, at times running to several cents on headline contracts. Those reports are journalistic rather than systematic.

claimed_performance.metric: n/a
claimed_performance.source_note: No credible author's claim exists for this.

strategies.known_decay: Unmeasured. Spreads should narrow as the venues' participant bases overlap more, but the structural friction - different collateral, different regulatory status - is not going away quickly.
strategies.capacity_notes: Bounded by the thinner venue.
strategies.data_gap: Neither venue publishes historical order book data, and Kalshi purges settled markets. Cannot be backtested. Recording must begin now.
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Decisive, but with a favourable asymmetry that does not exist within a single venue.
strategies.shorting_leverage: No borrow. Both legs are collateralised positions.
strategies.redundancy: Distinct from the within-venue no-arbitrage entries; this one carries cross-venue risk that those do not.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible. Two segmented pools of capital pricing the same outcome differently is a real and explicable phenomenon, not a claim that someone is behaving irrationally.
strategies.arb_type_justification: NOT riskless, despite appearances, and scepticism is warranted here. Three things break the identity: the two contracts may resolve on different sources or at different times, so a hedged position can lose on both legs; Polymarket settles in USDC on-chain with its own custody and resolution-dispute risk via UMA; and capital is trapped on two venues in two forms of money, so a failure at either end is an unhedged total loss on that leg. This is a statistical arbitrage wearing a riskless costume.

venues.us_retail_accessible: Yes - CFTC-designated, available in Florida and California.

VERIFY BEFORE RELYING ON THIS. Polymarket's availability to US persons has changed repeatedly and may differ by state and market category. This is a legal question, not a technical one, and it should be confirmed directly rather than assumed from any secondary source including this entry.

strategies.capital_required: The worst capital profile in the catalogue: funds must sit idle on BOTH venues simultaneously, in USD on one and USDC on the other, because neither transfer can be completed inside an opportunity window. Effective capital requirement is roughly double the position size, and the idle balance is exposed to venue risk continuously rather than only during trades.
strategies.fee_model: Kalshi taker: roundup(0.07 x C x P x (1-P)); maker roundup(0.0175 x C x P x (1-P)). Polymarket: fee = C x rate x p x (1-p) with MAKERS CHARGED ZERO in every category, and taker rates of 0.07 crypto, 0.05 sports/economics/culture/weather, 0.04 finance/politics/tech, and 0.00 geopolitics. Polymarket adds on-chain gas and USDC conversion costs; neither venue charges deposit or withdrawal fees.
strategies.net_edge_analysis: THE ASYMMETRY BETWEEN THE TWO FEE SCHEDULES IS THE WHOLE OPPORTUNITY. Polymarket charges makers nothing at all, and charges takers nothing in geopolitics. Kalshi charges everyone. The cheapest possible structure is therefore a resting order on Polymarket paired with a taker order on Kalshi, which incurs only the Kalshi side of the fee: 0.07*p*(1-p), or 1.75 cents at p=0.50 and 0.33 cents at p=0.05. That is half the cost of the equivalent two-leg trade within Kalshi alone. A politics contract taken on both sides costs 0.07*p*(1-p) on Kalshi plus 0.04*p*(1-p) on Polymarket, or 2.75 cents at p=0.50. The reported multi-cent divergences during the 2024 election cycle would have cleared that hurdle comfortably, which suggests the opportunity is real - though a single election cycle is not a sample.
strategies.return_per_capital_per_day: Materially worse than the headline edge implies, because capital is committed on two venues at once. A 3-cent net edge on a 30-day contract returns roughly 37% annualised on the capital in the trade, but only about 18% on total capital deployed once the idle mirror balance on the second venue is counted. Every analysis of this trade that quotes the first number and not the second is wrong.
strategies.execution_risk: Highest of any entry in this catalogue. One leg filling without the other leaves a naked directional position split across two venues in two currencies. Added to that is resolution risk: if the two contracts resolve on different sources or on different dates, a position that looked hedged can lose on both sides. The resolution-criteria comparison must be done by reading both contracts in full, every time.
strategies.latency_note: Cross-venue divergences persist for minutes to hours because the capital that would close them cannot move quickly. This is the rare case where the friction that creates the opportunity also protects it from faster participants.
strategies.reason: The fee asymmetry is real and favourable, and the latency requirement is human-scale, but it must be restricted to contracts whose resolution criteria have been read and verified as identical, and the doubled capital requirement has to be in the return calculation from the start.

preliminary_estimate.expected_annual_return_over_bh: Unknown without recorded data. Plausibly attractive during high-attention events, near zero the rest of the time.
preliminary_estimate.expected_drawdown: Bounded per trade if resolution criteria match; unbounded if they do not
preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes Polymarket access is legally available, maker execution on the Polymarket leg, and verified matching resolution. The legal question is the gating one and I cannot resolve it.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: No published claim exists. Journalistic accounts of 2024 election divergences describe gross spreads and do not net fees or account for doubled capital.

tweaks.change: Rest the order on the Polymarket side and take on Kalshi, never the reverse.
tweaks.why: Polymarket's maker fee is zero, so this halves the total fee versus taking on both. It follows directly from the published schedules rather than from any fitting.
tweaks.disproof: If Polymarket maker fills are too rare during the brief windows when divergences exist, the fee saving is unreachable and the trade must pay taker on both sides.

tweaks.change: Concentrate on Polymarket's geopolitics category, where the taker fee is zero.
tweaks.why: A fee-free leg is the single largest cost improvement available in the entire event contract section.
tweaks.disproof: If Kalshi does not list matching geopolitics contracts with identical resolution criteria, there is nothing to pair against.

tweaks.change: Require a written resolution-criteria match check before any order, and skip any pair where the sources differ.
tweaks.why: Addresses the failure mode that converts this from hedged to naked. A control, not a return enhancement.
tweaks.disproof: n/a

strategies.name: Signed Order Flow Imbalance
strategies.one_line: Predict short-horizon price movement from the imbalance between buyer-initiated and seller-initiated volume.
strategies.hypothesis: Signed transaction volume - buy market orders positive, sell market orders negative - measures the net pressure informed traders are applying. Because a large informed order is broken into pieces and executed over time, the imbalance it creates predicts the remainder of its own price impact. The mechanism is mechanical rather than behavioural and is one of the most robustly documented relationships in market microstructure.
strategies.universe: Liquid US equities or index futures with reconstructable trade and quote data.
strategies.entry_rule: Reconstruct signed order flow by classifying each trade against the prevailing quote (Lee-Ready or tick rule). Aggregate over a short window. Enter long when cumulative signed flow over the window exceeds a positive threshold, short when below a negative one.
strategies.exit_rule: Exit after a fixed horizon of minutes, or when cumulative flow reverses sign.
strategies.position_sizing: Fixed size scaled inversely by recent volatility. Position limits must be tight because holding periods are short and the edge per trade is small.

strategies.replication_notes: Chan gives a codeable order-flow strategy using ITCH message data. The underlying relationship between order flow and price impact is extensively documented in the microstructure literature and is not in dispute.

claimed_performance.metric: not stated in a comparable form
claimed_performance.value: Chan presents the strategy without a headline annualised figure in a form directly comparable to the other entries here.
claimed_performance.source_note: Author's demonstration rather than a performance claim.

strategies.known_decay: Order flow prediction at short horizons is the core business of professional market makers and high-frequency firms. Any edge at sub-minute horizons is comprehensively arbitraged. Longer horizons of 15-60 minutes are less contested but also much weaker.
strategies.capacity_notes: Very small. The edge decays with position size because the trade is itself adding to the impact it is predicting.
strategies.data_gap: Requires tick-level trade and quote data, which is explicitly unavailable locally. NYSE TAQ through WRDS is the academic route at institutional pricing; Polygon and Databento sell retail tick data at roughly $200-2000/month depending on depth and history. Storage and processing are substantial additional costs beyond the subscription.
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Decisive. At minute-scale holding periods the per-trade edge is measured in basis points and is smaller than a retail round-trip cost.
strategies.shorting_leverage: Requires intraday shorting with locates available continuously.
strategies.redundancy: No overlap with the catalogue's other entries, but note that the project's existing finding on large price gaps fading in microcaps is an adjacent microstructure result and the two may share a liquidity-provision mechanism.
strategies.common_sense: The mechanism is sound and well established. Whether a retail participant can capture any of it is a separate question, and the answer is probably not at the horizons where the edge is strongest.
strategies.reason: Blocked on tick data, and even unblocked it sits near the boundary where retail execution costs exceed the available edge. Low priority relative to everything else here.

preliminary_estimate.expected_annual_return_over_bh: Near zero net at retail cost levels
preliminary_estimate.rough_sharpe: Potentially high gross, near zero net
preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes retail commissions and spreads and no co-location. The gross-to-net gap here is larger than in any other entry.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Chan makes no directly comparable claim. My scepticism is about retail execution rather than about his result.

strategies.name: Buy-on-Gap Mean Reversion in Stocks
strategies.one_line: Buy stocks that open sharply below their previous low and sell them at the close the same day.
strategies.hypothesis: A large downward opening gap in the absence of fundamental news is largely forced selling - margin calls, fund redemptions, stop orders triggering in thin pre-market trade. The seller needs immediacy and pays for it. A buyer supplying that liquidity at the open is paid as the price recovers through the session. The same liquidity-provision mechanism as the cross-sectional reversal entries, applied to a more extreme and more identifiable event.
strategies.universe: Chan applies it to a liquid index universe; the effect is documented as strongest in small and illiquid names.
strategies.entry_rule: At the open of day t, buy stocks whose open is below the previous day's low by more than a multiple of the trailing 90-day standard deviation of close-to-close returns. Chan uses an entry z-score of 0.1 applied to that standard deviation, and additionally ranks candidates to select the most extreme.
strategies.exit_rule: Liquidate the entire position at the close of the same day.
strategies.position_sizing: Equal weight across qualifying names, gross exposure divided by a fixed maximum position count.

claimed_performance.metric: APR / Sharpe
claimed_performance.value: Chan reports favourable Sharpe ratios for gap strategies; the FSTX futures gap momentum variant he details separately returns 13% APR at Sharpe 1.4.
claimed_performance.source_note: Author's claim, gross of costs.

strategies.known_decay: Substantial, and this project has already measured it directly.
strategies.capacity_notes: Constrained to the point of being the defining problem - see redundancy.
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Severe. Entry at the open on a gapping stock is the widest spread available anywhere in the equity session.
strategies.shorting_leverage: The symmetric short-the-gap-up version requires borrow, and in microcaps borrow is typically unavailable at any price.
strategies.redundancy: DIRECT OVERLAP WITH AN ESTABLISHED PROJECT FINDING. This project has already determined that large price gaps fade sharply but only in microcaps, which cannot be borrowed. That finding substantially pre-empts this entry. It is retained in the catalogue for two reasons: the long-only version does not require borrow and so is not disposed of by the borrow constraint, and Chan's specific entry rule - gapping below the previous day's LOW rather than below the previous close - is a different and stricter condition than a raw gap measure, which may select a different population. Neither reason is strong. Treat this as largely settled unless the long-only microcap variant is specifically of interest.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible mechanism, but the project's own prior evidence should outweigh the published claim here.
strategies.reason: Pre-empted by the project's existing finding that gap fades are a microcap-only phenomenon in names that cannot be borrowed. Re-testing it would mostly reproduce work already done, and the information gained per day of effort is low.

preliminary_estimate.expected_annual_return_over_bh: Near zero in a liquid universe; positive but untradeable in microcaps
preliminary_estimate.rough_sharpe: Under 0.3 net in any tradeable universe
preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes the project's prior finding holds, 0.15% round trip at the open, liquid universe.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Chan's favourable figures are gross and, on the evidence this project has already gathered, concentrated in a universe that cannot actually be traded on the short side.

strategies.name: Turn-of-Month Seasonality
strategies.one_line: Hold the equity index only over the last trading day of the month and the first few of the next, and stay in cash the rest of the time.
strategies.hypothesis: Equity returns have historically clustered in a narrow window around the month boundary. The usual explanations are mechanical cash-flow timing: pension and payroll contributions arrive at month end and are invested, index funds rebalance, and performance reporting dates create window-dressing incentives. This is one of the few calendar effects with a mechanism that names an identifiable flow rather than merely observing a pattern in a date field - which matters, because calendar effects are the single most data-snooping-prone category in this entire catalogue.
strategies.universe: A broad US equity index or its ETF proxy.
strategies.entry_rule: Enter at the close of the last trading day of the month minus one. Chan discusses seasonal specifications of this type in Quantitative Trading 2e, Chapter 7.
strategies.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the third trading day of the new month.
strategies.position_sizing: Full index exposure during the window, cash otherwise. Approximately 4 of 21 trading days in the market.

data_required.history_needed: 30+ years - a calendar effect needs many independent month-boundaries to have any power

published.title: A Monthly Effect in Stock Returns

strategies.replication_notes: Widely replicated and widely doubted. Chan (2021) devotes a section of Chapter 7 to seasonal strategies and is explicit that they are the category most vulnerable to data-snooping bias, because the number of possible calendar specifications is enormous and nothing constrains the search.

claimed_performance.metric: share of total return
claimed_performance.value: Ariel's original finding was that essentially all of the market's cumulative return accrued in the first half of the month. Later turn-of-month studies attribute a large majority of index return to the 4-day boundary window.
claimed_performance.source_note: Author's claim. The original sample is 18 years, which is roughly 216 independent month-boundaries - a far smaller effective sample than the daily observation count suggests.

strategies.known_decay: Well documented as having weakened. The effect was published in 1988 and has had 38 years of exposure - the longest of any entry in this catalogue. McLean and Pontiff's decay estimate applies with full force. Several studies since 2000 find the effect substantially attenuated or absent in US large caps.
strategies.capacity_notes: Unlimited - it trades an index.
strategies.turnover: 24 round trips per year on a single instrument - trivial
strategies.cost_sensitivity: Very low. Two trades a month on a liquid ETF is the cheapest profile in this catalogue.
strategies.shorting_leverage: None required; the strategy is long or flat.
strategies.redundancy: No overlap with other entries. Note that being out of the market 80% of the time makes this a fundamentally different risk proposition from buy-and-hold rather than a variant of it.
strategies.common_sense: Sensible on its face, but this is exactly where the common-sense test needs to cut both ways. The cash-flow mechanism is plausible and names a real flow. But the effect is also indistinguishable in form from the thousands of spurious calendar patterns that a search over date fields will produce, and it has the longest post-publication exposure of anything here. Plausible mechanism plus enormous search space plus 38 years of publicity is a combination that should lower confidence, not raise it.
strategies.reason: Cheap to test and nearly free to run, which makes the information-per-day-of-work ratio high - but it must be tested as a decay question on post-publication data only, not as a full-sample backtest, or the result is meaningless.

preliminary_estimate.expected_annual_return_over_bh: Probably negative versus buy-and-hold on post-1990 data. Being out of the market 80% of the time sacrifices a great deal of equity risk premium.
preliminary_estimate.rough_sharpe: 0.3-0.6, potentially higher than buy-and-hold because exposure is brief, while total return is lower
preliminary_estimate.assumptions: Assumes post-publication sample only and 0.02% round trip on a liquid ETF. I expect this to be worth a fraction of its original claim - the honest prior is that most of it was in-sample.

strategies.estimate_vs_claim: Ariel's claim that essentially all market return accrued in half the month was measured on an 18-year sample ending in 1981. I estimate the post-publication effect at a small fraction of that, and would not be surprised by zero. Where my estimate differs most from the source is the effective sample size: 18 years of month-boundaries is roughly 216 independent observations, not thousands of daily ones, and the original t-statistics were computed as though the latter were true.

tweaks.change: Test only on data after the 1988 publication date.
tweaks.why: Turns a snooping-prone in-sample result into a clean out-of-sample decay test. The local data window from 1998 is entirely post-publication, which makes this free to do.
tweaks.disproof: If the post-1988 effect is not statistically distinguishable from zero, the effect was in-sample and the entry should be closed.

tweaks.change: Test whether the effect is larger in markets with more concentrated pension contribution schedules, or in months following large net fund inflows.
tweaks.why: Directly tests the stated cash-flow mechanism rather than the date pattern. If the mechanism is real the effect should vary with the flow.
tweaks.disproof: If the effect is flat across flow conditions, the cash-flow story is decoration on a date pattern and the entry is data-mined.

tweaks.change: Compare against a matched set of randomly chosen 4-day windows to establish a null distribution.
tweaks.why: Gives an empirical false-positive rate for a calendar effect of this size, which is the correction Harvey, Liu and Zhu argue is missing from this literature.
tweaks.disproof: If the turn-of-month window does not sit in the tail of that null distribution, it is not distinguishable from a randomly selected window.

tweaks.change: Vary the window boundaries.
tweaks.why: Calibration.
tweaks.disproof: If results are highly sensitive to a one-day shift, the specification was fitted - which for a calendar effect is close to fatal.
